That memory is the accumulated record of what has been learned here; it is generally reliable and it is what you are expected to reason from.

  Three things are happening at once:

      price-sensitive SMB accounts

  1 inherited memory before committing. Name it by id. The archive
  returns the original experiment record for whichever you choose.

    simplify_onboarding · promotional_pricing · referral_incentive ·
    activation_messaging · enterprise_sales_assist

Name the memory you want verified (up to one, or none) and state the
action you currently intend. Answer with the structured object only.

answer.rationale:
Two of the three current problems are internal funnel decay (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%), and only one direction addresses both at their shared root: the onboarding path itself. Promotional pricing is the tempting response to the competitor, but memory_73 describes acquisition/revenue lift in a price-sensitive SMB segment — exactly the cohort that discount-driven acquisition tends to buy cheaply and lose quickly. Matching aggressive entry pricing also concedes the pricing frame to the competitor and taxes margin permanently, which conflicts with the sustainable long-term qualified revenue objective. Referral incentives (memory_57) work in established customers and do nothing for a decaying activation funnel. Enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) is a real strength but is orthogonal to this quarter's regression and would leave the self-serve leak untouched. Activation messaging (memory_91) treats the symptom one layer downstream of a broken onboarding flow; fixing the flow should propagate into activation anyway.

I am spending the single verification pull on memory_86 rather than memory_73 because memory_86 is the load-bearing claim for the action I actually intend to take, and it is the one whose wording worries me. It reports improved completion rates and time-to-value 'lifting early product adoption' — all upstream proxies, none of them qualified revenue. If the original record shows the lift was measured only at the completion-rate step, or on a cohort unlike our currently-regressing one, then my mechanism is weaker than the memory's summary implies and I would lean toward activation_messaging as the more directly evidenced intervention. memory_31 partially corroborates the direction (signup field reduction, durable first-week activation lift), but it is about a different step of the funnel, so it is not a true independent confirmation. Verifying memory_73 would not change my decision, since I would decline margin-eroding discounting even if its record were pristine — so that pull would buy no information.
